tips.title: Respiration releases energy, never makes it
tips.body: Energy cannot be **created**. Respiration **releases** energy that was already stored in **glucose**. *Respiration produces energy* and *makes energy* are both marked wrong, however good the rest of the answer is. The verb is **release** — or **transfer**.

tips.title: Respiration is not breathing
tips.body: **Breathing** moves air in and out of the lungs. **Respiration** is a chemical reaction in **every living cell**, all the time, including in plants and in bacteria that never breathe. A question about respiration is never answered by describing the ribs and diaphragm.

tips.title: Two anaerobic equations, two organisms
tips.body: In **animal muscle**: glucose → **lactic acid**. In **yeast and plants**: glucose → **ethanol + carbon dioxide**. Both release **less** energy than aerobic respiration. Giving the yeast products for a human muscle question is the standard lost mark.

tips.title: Soda lime is what makes the reading mean oxygen
tips.body: In a respirometer the organisms take in oxygen **and** give out carbon dioxide, so the volume would barely change. **Soda lime absorbs the carbon dioxide**, so the only change left is the **oxygen used** — which is why the liquid moves at all.

tips.title: Rate is distance or volume over time
tips.body: $\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{time}}$ — millimetres moved per minute, or cm³ of gas per minute. Keep the unit with the number, and check the direction: **more** respiration means the liquid moves **further** in the same time.

steps.title: What respiration is
steps.body:
**Cellular respiration is an exothermic reaction which occurs continuously in living cells to release energy for metabolic processes.** That is the specification's own sentence, and every phrase in it is examinable.

- **Exothermic** — it **transfers energy to the surroundings**, which is why you get warm when you exercise.
- **Continuously** — it never stops. A cell that stops respiring dies.
- **In living cells** — *all* of them: animal, plant, fungal and bacterial.
- **Releases energy** — the energy was already **stored in glucose**. Respiration does not create it.

**The verb matters more than anything else here.** Energy cannot be created or destroyed, so respiration **releases** or **transfers** energy that was already there. *Produces energy* and *makes energy* are marked wrong even when the rest of the sentence is perfect.

**What the energy is for** — the *metabolic processes* the spec mentions:

- **building larger molecules from smaller ones**, such as proteins from amino acids
- **muscle contraction**, so that you can move
- **keeping a constant body temperature** in mammals and birds
- **active transport**, moving substances against a concentration gradient

**And respiration is not breathing.** Breathing — properly called **ventilation** — moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a **chemical reaction inside cells**. Plants respire and have no lungs; so do bacteria. The two words get confused constantly, and a question about respiration is never answered by describing the diaphragm.

steps.title: Aerobic respiration
steps.body:
**Aerobic respiration uses oxygen**, and it is how cells release energy almost all of the time.

**The word equation:**

$$\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$$

**The balanced symbol equation:**

$$\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O}$$

**Check it yourself rather than trusting the memory of it.** On the left: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, and $6 + 12 = 18$ oxygen. On the right: 6 carbon, 12 hydrogen, and $12 + 6 = 18$ oxygen. Balanced — and doing that check takes ten seconds in an exam.

**Where it happens.** In the **mitochondria**, which is why cells that need a lot of energy — muscle cells, sperm cells, the cells lining the small intestine — contain so many of them.

**Why aerobic respiration is the preferred route**: it releases **much more energy per glucose molecule** than the anaerobic alternatives, because the glucose is broken down **completely** into carbon dioxide and water. Nothing usable is left over.

**That last point is the explanation, not just a fact.** Anaerobic respiration releases less energy **because the breakdown is incomplete** — the products still contain chemical energy. Lactic acid and ethanol can both be broken down further, which is exactly why they still hold energy that aerobic respiration would have released.

steps.title: Anaerobic respiration
steps.body:
**Anaerobic respiration happens without oxygen**, and there are **two different versions** depending on the organism.

**In animal muscle**, during hard exercise when the blood cannot deliver oxygen fast enough:

$$\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}$$

**In yeast and in plant cells** — this is **fermentation**:

$$\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}$$

**Giving the wrong pair is the standard lost mark.** A question about a sprinter wants **lactic acid**; a question about bread or beer wants **ethanol and carbon dioxide**. They are not interchangeable.

**Both release much less energy than aerobic respiration**, and for one reason: the **breakdown of glucose is incomplete**. Lactic acid and ethanol are both still energy-containing molecules — which is precisely why ethanol burns and why lactic acid can be converted back to glucose.

**Oxygen debt.** Lactic acid **builds up** in the muscles during hard exercise, causing fatigue and pain. Afterwards you keep **breathing hard and deeply** for several minutes even though you have stopped: that extra oxygen is needed to break the lactic acid down. The amount required is the **oxygen debt**, and the lactic acid is carried in the blood to the **liver**, where it is converted back into **glucose**.

**So the panting after a race is not left over from the race.** It is paying for a reaction that has not finished, which is a much better answer than *to get oxygen back*.

**Why anaerobic respiration is used at all**, given it is so much less efficient: it can release energy **very quickly** and **without oxygen**, which lets a muscle keep working when the lungs and heart cannot keep up.

steps.title: Comparing the two
steps.body:
**Spec point 8.10 asks you to compare**, and a comparison needs **both sides of each point**, not a list of facts about one.

**The four points of comparison:**

1. **Oxygen.** Aerobic **requires** it; anaerobic does **not**.
2. **Products.** Aerobic gives **carbon dioxide and water**; anaerobic gives **lactic acid** in animals, or **ethanol and carbon dioxide** in yeast and plants.
3. **Energy released.** Aerobic releases **much more** per glucose molecule.
4. **Breakdown of glucose.** Aerobic is **complete**; anaerobic is **incomplete** — and this is the **reason** for point 3.

**Write comparisons as comparisons.** *Aerobic respiration releases a lot of energy* is a statement about one process. *Aerobic respiration releases **much more** energy per glucose molecule **than** anaerobic respiration, **because** the glucose is broken down completely* is a comparison with a reason. The command word **compare** is asking for the second kind of sentence.

**What the two have in common** is worth knowing too, because it is sometimes asked: both **start with glucose**, both **release energy**, and both happen **in living cells**.

**When each is used.** Aerobic respiration runs almost all the time. Anaerobic respiration takes over in muscle only when demand outruns the oxygen supply — during a sprint, for example — and it is a **short-term** measure, because the lactic acid accumulates and must eventually be dealt with.

steps.title: Core practical: the rate of respiration
steps.body:
**This is core practical 5**, and it uses a **respirometer**.

**How it works:**

1. Living organisms — usually **germinating peas**, sometimes small invertebrates — go in a sealed tube.
2. **Soda lime** is added, which **absorbs carbon dioxide**.
3. The tube connects to a **capillary tube** containing a drop of coloured liquid.
4. As the organisms respire they **take in oxygen**, and the carbon dioxide they release is **absorbed by the soda lime**. The volume of gas inside therefore **falls**, and the liquid **moves towards the organisms**.
5. Measure **how far the drop moves in a fixed time**.

**Soda lime is the whole trick.** Without it, oxygen would be taken in and carbon dioxide given out in roughly equal volumes, so the pressure would barely change and the drop would hardly move. Absorbing the carbon dioxide leaves the **oxygen used** as the only change — so the movement measures respiration.

**The control tube** contains **glass beads** instead of organisms, and everything else is identical. Any movement in that tube is caused by **changes in temperature or air pressure** in the room rather than by respiration, so it shows how much of the reading is not the thing being measured.

$$\text{rate} = \frac{\text{distance moved}}{\text{time}}$$

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Release, not produce.** Energy cannot be created, so respiration **releases** or **transfers** energy that was already **stored in glucose**. This is marked strictly, and rightly: the wrong verb signals a wrong model of what a chemical reaction does.

**The energy difference has a cause, and the cause is the mark.** Anaerobic respiration releases less energy **because the glucose is only partly broken down**. The evidence is in the products: **ethanol burns** and **lactic acid can be converted back into glucose**, so both clearly still contain chemical energy. Aerobic respiration breaks glucose **completely**, to carbon dioxide and water, leaving nothing usable behind.

**Keep the two anaerobic equations with their organisms.** **Muscle → lactic acid. Yeast and plants → ethanol and carbon dioxide.** The commonest error in this topic is giving a sprinter the yeast products. Note too that anaerobic respiration in **yeast** produces carbon dioxide while in **muscle** it produces none — which is why a question about gas given off distinguishes them.

**Oxygen debt is about an unfinished reaction.** The heavy breathing after exercise is not left over from the effort; it is supplying the oxygen needed to **break down the lactic acid** that built up, which is carried to the **liver** and converted back into **glucose**. Saying *to get oxygen back into the blood* misses what the oxygen is actually for.

**Soda lime is what makes the respirometer work at all.** Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out are roughly equal volumes, so without the soda lime the gas volume would barely change and the drop would hardly move. **Absorbing the carbon dioxide** leaves **oxygen uptake** as the only volume change. A student who can say that has understood the apparatus rather than memorised it.

**The control tube is not a spare.** Glass beads do not respire, so any movement in that tube must come from **room temperature or air pressure** changing. It measures the error, which is exactly what a control is for.

**And respiration is enzyme-controlled.** So warming the peas speeds it up — but only **to an optimum**. Past that the enzymes **denature** and the rate **falls**. A graph of rate against temperature in this practical has the same shape as the enzyme graph, and saying so links the two topics.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Respiration is an exothermic reaction, occurring continuously in living cells, that releases energy for metabolic processes.**
- It **releases** energy stored in **glucose** — it never **produces** or **makes** it.
- **Respiration is not breathing.** Breathing is ventilation of the lungs; respiration happens in **every living cell**.
- Energy is needed for **building larger molecules**, **muscle contraction**, **keeping warm**, and **active transport**.
- **Aerobic**: $\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$.
- Symbol equation: $\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \rightarrow 6CO_2 + 6H_2O}$ — 6 C, 12 H and 18 O on each side.
- Aerobic respiration happens in the **mitochondria**.
- **Anaerobic in muscle**: $\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}$.
- **Anaerobic in yeast and plants**: $\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}$ — **fermentation**.
- Anaerobic respiration releases **much less** energy **because the glucose is broken down incompletely**.
- **Oxygen debt**: the oxygen needed afterwards to **break down the lactic acid** that built up.
- Lactic acid is carried to the **liver** and converted back into **glucose**.
- **Core practical 5**: a **respirometer** measures how far a drop of liquid moves in a fixed time.
- **Soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide**, so the volume change measures **oxygen used**.
- A **control tube of glass beads** shows movement caused by **temperature or pressure**, not respiration.
- $\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{distance moved}}{\text{time}}$, and respiration is **enzyme-controlled**, so it has an **optimum temperature**.

questions.prompt: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration, and explain why a sprinter respires anaerobically during a race and breathes heavily afterwards.
questions.solution:
The two processes differ on four points, and each is worth stating as a **comparison** rather than as a fact about one of them.

First, **oxygen**. Aerobic respiration **requires** oxygen; anaerobic respiration does **not**. Second, the **products**. Aerobic respiration gives **carbon dioxide and water**: $\text{glucose} + \text{oxygen} \rightarrow \text{carbon dioxide} + \text{water}$. Anaerobic respiration gives different products in different organisms — in **animal muscle**, $\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{lactic acid}$; in **yeast and plants**, $\text{glucose} \rightarrow \text{ethanol} + \text{carbon dioxide}$.

Third, the **energy released**. Aerobic respiration releases **much more energy per glucose molecule** than either anaerobic route. Fourth — and this is the reason for the third — the **breakdown of glucose** is **complete** in aerobic respiration but **incomplete** in anaerobic respiration. The evidence is in the products themselves: **ethanol burns**, and **lactic acid can be converted back into glucose**, so both clearly still contain chemical energy that has not been released. Aerobic respiration leaves only carbon dioxide and water, from which nothing further can be obtained.

During a sprint, the muscles are working so hard that the heart and lungs **cannot deliver oxygen fast enough** to keep up with demand. Rather than stop, the muscle cells switch to **anaerobic respiration**, which releases energy **quickly and without oxygen**. The cost is that far less energy comes from each glucose molecule, and that **lactic acid accumulates** in the muscles, causing fatigue and pain. It is a short-term measure only.

Afterwards, the sprinter continues to breathe **hard and deeply** for several minutes even though the effort has stopped. That extra oxygen is the **oxygen debt**: the oxygen needed to **break down the lactic acid** that built up. The lactic acid is carried in the blood to the **liver**, where it is converted back into **glucose**. So the heavy breathing is not simply recovery from exertion — it is supplying the oxygen for a reaction that the race left unfinished.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would use a respirometer to investigate the effect of temperature on the rate of respiration in germinating peas, and explain how you would make the results valid.
questions.solution:
I would place a known mass of **germinating peas** in a sealed tube together with **soda lime**, and connect the tube to a **capillary tube** containing a drop of coloured liquid. The whole apparatus would stand in a **water bath** at a set temperature.

As the peas respire they **take in oxygen** and give out **carbon dioxide**. On their own these two would be roughly equal volumes, so the pressure inside would barely change and the drop would hardly move. The **soda lime** is what makes the experiment work: it **absorbs the carbon dioxide**, so the only remaining change in volume is the **oxygen used**. The gas volume therefore falls and the drop moves **towards the peas**, and the distance it moves is a measure of respiration.

To investigate temperature I would repeat the measurement with the water bath set to a range of values — for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C — allowing the apparatus time to reach each temperature before starting. For each one I would record **how far the drop moves in a fixed time**, say five minutes, and calculate $\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{distance moved}}{\text{time}}$ in mm per minute. Using a **rate** rather than a raw distance matters if the timings are not identical, and it makes higher mean faster.

Several things must be kept the **same**: the **mass of peas**, the **volume of the apparatus**, the **time** allowed, and the **quantity of soda lime**. I would also reset the drop to a starting position before each run.

The most important refinement is a **control tube** containing **glass beads** instead of peas, identical in every other way and in the same water bath. Glass beads do **not respire**, so any movement of liquid in that tube must be caused by the **air expanding or contracting** as the temperature or the room's air pressure changes. Subtracting that movement from the readings removes an error that would otherwise grow with temperature and be mistaken for faster respiration — which is precisely what would make the results **invalid**.

I would expect the rate to **rise** with temperature at first, because the molecules have more **kinetic energy** and collide more often. Respiration is **enzyme-controlled**, though, so past an **optimum** the enzymes **denature**: their **active sites change shape**, substrate no longer fits, and the rate **falls steeply**. The graph should therefore have the same shape as any enzyme activity graph, which is a useful check that the results are behaving as biology predicts.

criteria.text: Describes the apparatus: germinating peas and soda lime in a sealed tube connected to a capillary tube with a drop of coloured liquid.
Explains that soda lime absorbs carbon dioxide so the volume change measures oxygen uptake.
Describes varying temperature using water baths, and measuring how far the drop moves in a fixed time.
Explains the control tube of glass beads, which shows movement caused by temperature or pressure rather than respiration.
Calculates a rate as distance divided by time, and predicts a rise to an optimum followed by a fall as enzymes denature.

questions.modelAnswer:
I would place a known mass of **germinating peas** in a sealed tube together with **soda lime**, and connect the tube to a **capillary tube** containing a drop of coloured liquid. The whole apparatus would stand in a **water bath** at a set temperature.

As the peas respire they **take in oxygen** and give out **carbon dioxide**. On their own these two would be roughly equal volumes, so the pressure inside would barely change and the drop would hardly move. The **soda lime** is what makes the experiment work: it **absorbs the carbon dioxide**, so the only remaining change in volume is the **oxygen used**. The gas volume therefore falls and the drop moves **towards the peas**, and the distance it moves is a measure of respiration.

To investigate temperature I would repeat the measurement with the water bath set to a range of values — for example 10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 °C — allowing the apparatus time to reach each temperature before starting. For each one I would record **how far the drop moves in a fixed time**, say five minutes, and calculate $\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{distance moved}}{\text{time}}$ in mm per minute. Using a **rate** rather than a raw distance matters if the timings are not identical, and it makes higher mean faster.

Several things must be kept the **same**: the **mass of peas**, the **volume of the apparatus**, the **time** allowed, and the **quantity of soda lime**. I would also reset the drop to a starting position before each run.

The most important refinement is a **control tube** containing **glass beads** instead of peas, identical in every other way and in the same water bath. Glass beads do **not respire**, so any movement of liquid in that tube must be caused by the **air expanding or contracting** as the temperature or the room's air pressure changes. Subtracting that movement from the readings removes an error that would otherwise grow with temperature and be mistaken for faster respiration — which is precisely what would make the results **invalid**.

I would expect the rate to **rise** with temperature at first, because the molecules have more **kinetic energy** and collide more often. Respiration is **enzyme-controlled**, though, so past an **optimum** the enzymes **denature**: their **active sites change shape**, substrate no longer fits, and the rate **falls steeply**. The graph should therefore have the same shape as any enzyme activity graph, which is a useful check that the results are behaving as biology predicts.

examTechnique.body:
One word decides several marks in this topic: respiration **releases** energy, it does not produce it. Fix that, and keep **breathing** and **respiration** apart, and most of the easy marks look after themselves.

For spec point 8.10 the command word is **compare**, so write sentences with two sides and a **because**. The fourth point of comparison — complete against incomplete breakdown — is the reason for the third, and stating that link is what lifts an answer.
examinerErrors: Writing that respiration **produces** or **makes** energy, rather than **releasing** energy stored in glucose.
Describing **breathing** when the question asked about **respiration**.
Giving **ethanol and carbon dioxide** as the products in a **human muscle**, where the product is **lactic acid**.
Stating that anaerobic respiration releases less energy without giving the reason: **incomplete breakdown** of glucose.
Explaining oxygen debt as *getting oxygen back*, rather than oxygen needed to **break down lactic acid**.
Leaving **soda lime** out of a respirometer description, so the apparatus described would barely work.
Treating the **glass bead control** as a repeat reading rather than a measure of temperature and pressure effects.
Forgetting that respiration is **enzyme-controlled**, and predicting that the rate rises indefinitely with temperature.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer uses the verb **release** without thinking about it, and treats the energy difference between the two routes as something to **explain** rather than state: anaerobic respiration leaves **lactic acid or ethanol**, which still contain chemical energy, so the breakdown is **incomplete**. It keeps the two anaerobic routes attached to their organisms, and can use the difference — **yeast gives off carbon dioxide, muscle does not** — to interpret an unfamiliar experiment. On oxygen debt it says what the oxygen is **for**, and names the **liver**. On the practical it explains **soda lime** as the reason the drop moves at all, treats the **glass bead tube** as a measurement of error rather than a spare, and predicts an **optimum** because respiration is **enzyme-controlled**.
